title: Why You Should Avoid Sending Students To The Principal the-principal/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues, somewhat counterintuitively, that referring students to the principal for routine misbehavior weakens rather than strengthens a teacher's classroom management. He gives three reasons: it signals to the class that the teacher isn't the ultimate authority, it erodes the teacher's own confidence in handling misbehavior, and it emboldens the student because a principal's tools (lectures, threats) are no more effective than the classroom's and the student soon returns knowing the teacher couldn't manage them independently. He clarifies that principals can still meaningfully influence classroom behavior, but indirectly through leadership, expectations, and school-wide order rather than by directly disciplining referred students. He carves out exceptions for genuinely dangerous or suspendable behavior, and even then insists the teacher stay actively involved—leading meetings and contacting parents—rather than handing the situation off entirely.
points: Referring students to the principal for routine misbehavior signals to the class that the teacher isn't the ultimate authority.
Relying on the principal erodes a teacher's own confidence and skill at handling challenging behavior directly.
A returning referred student knows the teacher couldn't manage them alone, which emboldens rather than deters further misbehavior.
Principals influence classroom behavior effectively but indirectly, through leadership, expectations, and school-wide order.
Genuinely dangerous or suspendable behavior is an exception, but the teacher should still stay actively involved in the process.
quotes: Contrary to what many believe, the role of principal doesn’t include directly influencing behavior in your classroom.
When you refer a student to the principal you’re communicating to that student—as well as to the rest of your class—that you’re not the ultimate authority of your classroom.
Relying on your principal to step in and handle what is your responsibility can be devastating to your self-confidence.
The difference is that now they’ll know you’re unable to manage them by yourself—or at all for that matter. Rather than dissuading misbehavior, it emboldens it.

A good principal can have influence on behavior—tremendously so. But it comes indirectly through their leadership, their organizational skills, their expectations of teachers, and their commitment to excellence.
Any dangerous, harmful, or potentially suspendable behavior should be documented and brought to your principal’s attention immediately.
You must show them that you care enough, that they matter enough, for you to be there in the thick of it, right along with them.
